paragraphs.text: A delayed departure at a busy airport can affect flights across a whole continent, because aircraft and crews are often scheduled to fly several routes in a single day. For this reason, airports have become increasingly interested in finding out exactly where time is lost.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Much of the delay happens on the ground rather than in the air. Studies at large European airports found that aircraft often wait with their engines running for ten minutes or more between leaving the gate and taking off, burning fuel and adding to noise.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: One solution is to share information more closely. When airlines, air traffic controllers and ground staff use a single system to plan each departure, aircraft can stay at the gate with engines off until the runway is ready for them.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Passengers themselves also cause delays. Late arrivals at the gate, and bags that must be removed from the hold when a passenger fails to board, can hold up a flight for twenty minutes. Some airports now send text messages reminding passengers to go to the gate.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The results of these changes have been encouraging but uneven. Airports that introduced shared planning systems reduced average waiting times on the ground, yet delays caused by bad weather or strikes remain largely outside their control.
paragraphs.label: E
